Gen.name: Genesis
Gen.blurb: The opening book of the Pentateuch, combining primeval narrative with the family history of the patriarchs. It moves from accounts of creation, the flood, and the dispersion of nations to the stories of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, and supplies material echoed throughout both Testaments.
Gen.attribution: Jewish and Christian tradition attributes Genesis, with the rest of the Pentateuch, to Moses, and on that view it would date to roughly the fifteenth or thirteenth century BCE. Since the nineteenth century much critical scholarship has instead read it as a composite work drawing on earlier sources woven together over centuries and reaching its present form during or after the Babylonian exile in the sixth century BCE. The two positions remain the poles of ongoing debate.
Gen.setting: The narrative ranges from an unplaced account of origins to the ancestral movements of a single family across Mesopotamia, Canaan, and Egypt. Whatever its date of composition, the book addresses an Israelite audience seeking to understand its own origins, its relationship to neighboring peoples, and its claim to the land of Canaan. It presents itself as the prologue to the story of Israel that the following books continue.
Gen.themes: Genesis is organized around a recurring formula introducing the generations of successive figures, giving the whole a genealogical spine. Its major concerns include creation and human origins, the disruption of order through wrongdoing, and the promises of land, descendants, and blessing made to the patriarchs. It alternates sweeping primeval episodes with intimate family drama, and its narratives are among the most heavily reused across the canon.

Exod.name: Exodus
Exod.blurb: Narrative and law recounting Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt and the covenant made at Sinai. It contains the plague accounts, the departure from Egypt, the giving of the Ten Commandments, and instructions for the tabernacle, and its sections are widely referenced elsewhere in Scripture.
Exod.attribution: Tradition attributes Exodus to Moses, placing its events and composition in the second millennium BCE. Critical scholarship generally regards it as a composite of earlier narrative and legal traditions edited into their present form over a long period, with final shaping often dated to the exilic or post-exilic era. Scholars also differ over whether the exodus reflects a historical event, and if so its scale and date, without consensus.
Exod.setting: The book is set in Egypt, the Sinai wilderness, and the mountain of Sinai, following Israel from oppression under Pharaoh to its constitution as a covenant people. It addresses an audience for whom the deliverance from Egypt functioned as a foundational national memory. The account frames Israel's identity, its law, and its worship as flowing from this defining departure.
Exod.themes: Exodus joins a dramatic rescue narrative to extensive legal and cultic material. Its central concerns include liberation from bondage, the covenant and its stipulations, the presence of the deity among the people, and the ordering of worship through the tabernacle. It moves from story to statute to sanctuary, and its imagery of deliverance and covenant recurs throughout later biblical texts.
outline: Israel in Egypt and the call of Moses (1–6)

Lev.name: Leviticus
Lev.blurb: A book of priestly law and ritual instruction, set at Sinai within the larger Exodus narrative. It details sacrificial procedures, purity regulations, the priesthood, and the festival calendar, and its statutes on holiness and offering are frequently cited in later biblical texts.
Lev.attribution: Tradition assigns Leviticus to Moses as part of the Pentateuch. Critical scholars generally associate its material with priestly circles and a distinct Holiness stratum, holding that these traditions were compiled and edited over an extended period, with much of the writing commonly dated to the exilic or post-exilic centuries. Traditional and critical datings thus differ by many centuries.
Lev.setting: The book is set entirely at Mount Sinai, presented as instruction delivered to Moses for the priests and the people. Its original audience is an Israelite community for whom questions of purity, sacrifice, and access to the sanctuary were central to communal life. It assumes the tabernacle just completed at the end of Exodus.
Lev.themes: Leviticus is dominated by the concept of holiness and the distinctions between clean and unclean, sacred and common. Its literary character is largely instructional, cataloguing offerings, priestly duties, purity laws, festivals, and the ethical demands of the Holiness Code. The refrain calling the people to be holy gives the collection its unifying frame.

Num.name: Numbers
Num.blurb: A blend of narrative, census records, and law tracing Israel's wilderness journey from Sinai toward the land of Canaan. It records the numbering of the tribes, episodes of rebellion, and further legal material, and takes its English name from the two censuses it reports.
Num.attribution: Tradition attributes Numbers to Moses within the Pentateuch. Critical scholarship treats it as a composite of narrative and priestly legal traditions assembled over time, with substantial priestly editing usually dated to the exilic or post-exilic period. The traditional Mosaic dating and the critical multi-source view remain the principal alternatives.
Num.setting: The book covers the wilderness generation, moving from Sinai through the desert to the plains of Moab opposite Canaan. It addresses an Israelite audience reflecting on the long delay between the exodus and the entry into the land. The narrative frame is the transition from one wilderness generation to the next.
Num.themes: Numbers interweaves organization for the march, recurring complaint and rebellion, and consequences of failure to trust. Its literary character alternates itineraries, census lists, and legal material with vivid narrative episodes such as the spies and Balaam. Themes of divine guidance, testing in the wilderness, and preparation for the land run throughout.
outline: Preparation at Sinai and the first census (1–10)
The second census and preparation for the land (26–36)

Deut.name: Deuteronomy
Deut.blurb: Presented as Moses' farewell addresses on the plains of Moab, restating the law before Israel enters Canaan. It reviews the wilderness period, renews the covenant, and sets out blessings and curses, and is one of the most frequently quoted Old Testament books in the New Testament.
Deut.attribution: Tradition presents Deuteronomy as Moses' own words. Many critical scholars connect a core of the book with the law scroll discovered during Josiah's reign in the late seventh century BCE, viewing it as the program behind that king's reforms, with framing material added later. Others argue for older traditions underlying the book, and the relationship of its composition to Mosaic authorship remains debated.
Deut.setting: The book is set on the plains of Moab, on the threshold of the promised land, cast as a series of speeches delivered shortly before Moses' death. Its rhetoric addresses a new generation about to enter Canaan, and many scholars see it also speaking to later audiences facing questions of covenant loyalty. It functions as both retrospect and charge.
Deut.themes: Deuteronomy is structured as covenant address, blending historical review, legal restatement, and exhortation. Its characteristic concerns include exclusive loyalty to one deity, centralized worship, love and obedience framed as covenant terms, and a scheme of blessing and curse tied to faithfulness. Its sermonic style and vocabulary strongly shaped the historical books that follow.

Josh.name: Joshua
Josh.blurb: A historical narrative describing Israel's entry into Canaan under Joshua's leadership after the death of Moses. It recounts the crossing of the Jordan, military campaigns, and the division of the land among the tribes, opening the section of books covering Israel's life in the land.
Josh.attribution: Tradition associates the book with Joshua himself. Modern scholarship more often treats it as part of a larger Deuteronomistic History spanning Joshua through Kings, compiled from earlier traditions and shaped by editors during the monarchy and exile. The extent to which its conquest accounts reflect a single rapid campaign is widely debated among historians and archaeologists.
Josh.setting: The narrative is set in Canaan at the transition from wilderness wandering to settlement. It addresses an Israelite readership interested in how the tribes came to occupy the land and how that occupation was understood as the fulfillment of earlier promises. The book presents the settlement as a unified national undertaking.
Josh.themes: Joshua combines campaign narrative with tribal geography and covenant reflection. Its major concerns include the taking and apportioning of the land, fidelity to covenant obligations, and the consequences of obedience and its lack. The book alternates dramatic episodes with detailed boundary lists and closes with a formal call to covenant loyalty.
outline: Entry and conquest of the land (1–12)
Division of the land among the tribes (13–21)
The eastern tribes and disputed altar (22)
Joshua's farewell and covenant at Shechem (23–24)

Judg.name: Judges
Judg.blurb: Historical narrative covering the period between the settlement of Canaan and the rise of the monarchy. It relates a recurring cycle of apostasy, oppression, and deliverance through a series of tribal leaders called judges, including the accounts of Deborah, Gideon, and Samson.
Judg.attribution: The book is anonymous; a strand of tradition associates it with Samuel. Critical scholarship generally regards it as part of the Deuteronomistic History, assembling older hero traditions within an editorial framework and reaching its present form during the monarchy or exile. Its individual stories are often thought to preserve considerably older material.
Judg.setting: The narrative is set in the pre-monarchic period, among loosely allied tribes without a central ruler. It addresses an audience reflecting on a turbulent era of external threats and internal disorder, and several passages frame that disorder against the later institution of kingship. The recurring refrain about the absence of a king signals this vantage point.
Judg.themes: Judges is built on a cyclical pattern of decline, oppression, cry for help, and deliverance, repeated with growing severity. Its literary character mixes terse annalistic notes with extended, often morally complex hero narratives. Themes of covenant unfaithfulness, deliverance through unlikely figures, and social breakdown dominate, culminating in accounts of near-anarchy.
outline: Incomplete conquest and the pattern set (1–2)
Micah's idol and the Danite migration (17–18)

Ruth.name: Ruth
Ruth.blurb: A short narrative set in the time of the judges, telling of a Moabite woman who settles among the people of Israel with her mother-in-law Naomi. The book closes with a genealogy linking Ruth to King David.
Ruth.attribution: The book is anonymous, though tradition has associated it with Samuel. Scholars differ over its date: some read it as an early tale set in the settlement period, while many place its composition later, in the monarchic or post-exilic era, in part because of its interest in a foreign woman's inclusion. The question remains open.
Ruth.setting: The story unfolds in Moab and Bethlehem during the period of the judges, amid famine and its aftermath. Its concern with a Moabite's acceptance into an Israelite family has led some to read it against later post-exilic debates over intermarriage and communal boundaries. The rural setting of harvest and kinship shapes the whole.
Ruth.themes: Ruth is a tightly crafted novella exploring loyalty, kinship obligation, and provision for the vulnerable. Its concerns include the practice of levirate marriage and redemption of family land, the welcome of an outsider, and the quiet workings of providence in ordinary events. The closing genealogy ties the domestic story to the wider royal history.
outline: The appeal at the threshing floor (3)
Redemption, marriage, and the Davidic genealogy (4)

1Sam.name: 1 Samuel
1Sam.blurb: Historical narrative covering Israel's transition from the era of the judges to the monarchy. It follows the prophet Samuel, the reign of Saul as the first king, and the rise of David; the books of Samuel were originally a single work later divided in two.
1Sam.attribution: The work is anonymous. Critical scholarship commonly treats Samuel as part of the Deuteronomistic History, drawing on older narrative sources, including material about the ark and about the rise of David, edited into its present form during the monarchy and exile. Tradition once linked the books with the prophet Samuel, though the narrative extends beyond his lifetime.
1Sam.setting: The narrative is set in Israel's shift from decentralized tribal leadership to a centralized kingship, amid pressure from the Philistines. It addresses an audience concerned with the origins, legitimacy, and risks of monarchy. The rival careers of Saul and David give the period its dramatic shape.
1Sam.themes: First Samuel weaves together prophetic vocation, the demand for a king, and the contested transfer of royal favor. Its concerns include the ambivalence of kingship, the role of the prophet alongside the king, and the reversal of the humble and the powerful. The narrative is marked by richly drawn characterization and mounting tension between Saul and David.
outline: Samuel's rise and the ark narrative (1–7)
The demand for a king and Saul's accession (8–12)
The rise of David and conflict with Saul (16–31)

2Sam.name: 2 Samuel
2Sam.blurb: The continuation of the Samuel narrative, focused on the reign of David over Judah and then all Israel. It records his consolidation of the kingdom, the covenant promise made to his house, and the crises within his family and court.
2Sam.attribution: Like 1 Samuel, the book is anonymous and is generally regarded by critical scholars as part of the Deuteronomistic History. It draws on older court narratives, including a well-known account of succession within David's household, edited into their present form over time. The division from 1 Samuel is a later feature of the textual tradition.
2Sam.setting: The narrative is set in David's united kingdom, with Jerusalem newly established as its political and religious center. It addresses an audience interested in the foundations of the Davidic dynasty and the tensions that beset it. Court intrigue and dynastic succession dominate the horizon.
2Sam.themes: Second Samuel joins accounts of consolidation and triumph to a candid record of failure and its consequences. Central concerns include the enduring promise to David's house, the effects of the king's wrongdoing on his family and realm, and the fragile politics of succession. Its court narrative is noted for psychological depth and moral realism.
outline: David king over Judah and Israel (1–5)
The ark, the dynastic promise, and victories (6–10)

1Kgs.name: 1 Kings
1Kgs.blurb: Historical narrative beginning with the death of David and the reign of Solomon, including the building of the temple in Jerusalem. It then traces the division of the kingdom and the parallel histories of Israel and Judah, introducing the prophet Elijah.
1Kgs.attribution: The book is anonymous and is usually treated as part of the Deuteronomistic History. It cites older annals and narrative sources and is generally thought to have reached its present form through editing during the late monarchy and exile. Tradition variously associated the compilation with prophetic circles; Kings was originally one book later divided in two.
1Kgs.setting: The narrative spans the united monarchy under Solomon and the early generations of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah. It addresses an audience, plausibly in or after the exile, reckoning with how the monarchy fared and why. The temple in Jerusalem stands at the center of its concerns.
1Kgs.themes: First Kings evaluates successive rulers against standards of covenant loyalty and centralized worship. Its concerns include the temple and its significance, the schism of the kingdom, and the emergence of prophets who confront kings. The Elijah narratives introduce a sustained conflict between prophetic word and royal power.
outline: Elijah and the house of Ahab (17–22)

2Kgs.name: 2 Kings
2Kgs.blurb: The continuation of the Kings narrative, following the divided monarchy to its end. It records the ministry of Elisha, the fall of the northern kingdom to Assyria, and the fall of Jerusalem and exile to Babylon, closing the historical sequence of Israel's monarchy.
2Kgs.attribution: The book is anonymous and, with 1 Kings, is generally regarded as part of the Deuteronomistic History, compiled from older annals and prophetic traditions. Many scholars posit an edition late in the monarchy updated during the exile, which would account for its closing events in the sixth century BCE. The precise stages of editing remain debated.
2Kgs.setting: The narrative carries the two kingdoms through their decline to destruction: Samaria falls to Assyria and Jerusalem to Babylon. It addresses an audience living with the aftermath of national catastrophe and seeking to understand it. The looming imperial powers of Assyria and Babylon frame the whole.
2Kgs.themes: Second Kings measures kings and peoples against covenant fidelity and offers the collapse of both kingdoms as the reckoning. Its concerns include prophetic intervention, cultic reform and relapse, and the interpretation of exile. The Elisha cycle and the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah stand out amid a generally downward trajectory.
outline: The fall of the northern kingdom (17)
Judah's final kings and the fall of Jerusalem (21–25)

1Chr.name: 1 Chronicles
1Chr.blurb: Historical narrative retelling Israel's history with an emphasis on genealogy, temple worship, and the line of David. It opens with extended genealogies from Adam onward before focusing on David's reign, covering much of the same period as Samuel and Kings from a distinct vantage point.
1Chr.attribution: Tradition associates Chronicles with Ezra the scribe. Critical scholarship generally regards it as the work of an anonymous writer or circle, commonly called the Chronicler, active in the post-exilic period, roughly the fifth or fourth century BCE. Whether Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah come from the same hand is itself debated.
1Chr.setting: Written for a post-exilic community in Judah under Persian rule, the book looks back on the monarchy from a later vantage. It addresses readers concerned with continuity between the restored community and its ancestral institutions, especially the temple. The genealogies anchor that community in a long remembered lineage.
1Chr.themes: First Chronicles reworks earlier history with strong interest in worship, priesthood, and the Davidic line. Its concerns include the legitimacy of the temple cult, the organization of Levites and singers, and an idealized portrait of David as its founder. The lengthy genealogies and cultic lists give it a markedly liturgical and archival character.
outline: Genealogies from Adam to the restoration (1–9)
The death of Saul and David's accession (10–12)
The ark and preparations for the temple (13–16)
The dynastic promise and David's wars (17–20)

2Chr.name: 2 Chronicles
2Chr.blurb: The continuation of Chronicles, following the reign of Solomon and the kings of Judah down to the Babylonian exile. It gives particular attention to the temple, its worship, and religious reforms, and ends with the decree of Cyrus permitting the return from exile.
2Chr.attribution: As with 1 Chronicles, tradition names Ezra while critical scholarship attributes the work to an anonymous post-exilic Chronicler of the fifth or fourth century BCE. The book draws on Samuel and Kings and other cited sources, reshaping them for its own purposes. Its relationship to Ezra-Nehemiah continues to be discussed.
2Chr.setting: The book addresses the post-exilic Judean community, presenting the history of the southern kingdom with the Jerusalem temple at its center. Its closing note about Cyrus points readers toward the restoration in which they live. The concerns of a temple-centered community shape the selection of material.
2Chr.themes: Second Chronicles focuses almost entirely on Judah and its temple, emphasizing worship, reform, and a pattern of immediate consequence for faithfulness or its lack. Its concerns include the building and use of the temple, the reforms of kings such as Hezekiah and Josiah, and a strong retributive framing of events. It largely omits the northern kingdom to keep the temple in view.
outline: The reign of Solomon and the temple (1–9)
The division and early kings of Judah (10–16)
The final kings, fall of Jerusalem, and Cyrus' decree (36)

Ezra.name: Ezra
Ezra.blurb: A post-exilic historical narrative recording the return of Jewish exiles from Babylon and the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. It includes documents in both Hebrew and Aramaic and describes Ezra's efforts to reestablish the law; it is closely connected to the book of Nehemiah.
Ezra.attribution: Tradition attributes the book to Ezra, and it incorporates first-person memoir material associated with him. Critical scholarship generally sees it as a compilation by a post-exilic editor drawing on memoirs, lists, and official documents, produced in the Persian period, roughly the fifth or fourth century BCE. In the Hebrew canon Ezra and Nehemiah form a single work.
Ezra.setting: The book is set in the early Persian period, following the decree permitting exiles to return and rebuild. It addresses a restored community in Judah reconstituting its worship and communal identity under imperial authority. The Aramaic documents reflect the administrative world of the Persian empire.
Ezra.themes: Ezra traces restoration through return, temple-building, and renewed commitment to the law. Its concerns include continuity with the pre-exilic community, the reestablishment of proper worship, and the maintenance of communal boundaries, including controversy over intermarriage. The book mixes narrative, official correspondence, and lists of returnees.

Neh.name: Nehemiah
Neh.blurb: A post-exilic historical narrative recounting the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and the community reforms that followed the return from exile. It draws substantially on first-person memoirs attributed to Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king.
Neh.attribution: The book preserves a first-person memoir attributed to Nehemiah, widely regarded as reflecting genuine reminiscences, set within an edited compilation. Critical scholarship places its final form in the Persian period, roughly the fifth or fourth century BCE, and often connects it editorially with Ezra. In the Hebrew tradition it was joined with Ezra as a single book.
Neh.setting: The narrative is set in Jerusalem under Persian rule, as a returned community works to secure and order the city. It addresses readers concerned with the physical and social restoration of the community after exile. The imperial court and provincial politics form the backdrop to Nehemiah's mission.
Neh.themes: Nehemiah centers on rebuilding, both of walls and of communal life, in the face of opposition. Its concerns include civic reconstruction, social justice within the community, covenant renewal, and observance of the law and its festivals. The memoir sections give the book an unusually personal and vivid voice.
outline: The community and public reading of the law (7–8)

Esth.name: Esther
Esth.blurb: A short narrative set in the Persian court, telling how a Jewish queen acts to avert the destruction of her people. It provides the account behind the festival of Purim, and notably does not mention God by name.
Esth.attribution: The book is anonymous. Critical scholarship generally regards it as a work of prose fiction or historical novella composed in the Persian or early Hellenistic period, roughly the fourth or third century BCE, whether or not it draws on any historical kernel. Its historicity is much debated, and the traditional and critical readings differ over how far it records actual events.
Esth.setting: The story is set in the Persian capital of Susa during the reign of a king identified with Xerxes. It addresses a diaspora Jewish audience living as a minority under foreign rule and concerned with survival and identity. The festival of Purim gives the book a clear communal function.
Esth.themes: Esther is a court tale of reversal, danger, and deliverance, marked by irony and a carefully plotted structure. Its concerns include the precariousness and resilience of a threatened people, the workings of providence conveyed without naming the deity, and the origins of a festival. The absence of any explicit reference to God is one of its most discussed features.
outline: Deliverance and the origin of Purim (8–10)

Job.name: Job
Job.blurb: A work of wisdom literature, largely in poetry framed by a prose narrative, exploring the problem of undeserved suffering. It presents the dialogues between Job and his companions and a series of speeches attributed to God, standing among the oldest and most debated texts in the wisdom tradition.
Job.attribution: The book is anonymous, and its date is unusually uncertain. Proposals range widely, from the pre-exilic period to the post-exilic centuries, with many scholars favoring a date around the exile or later on linguistic and thematic grounds. The relationship between the prose frame and the poetic core, and whether they come from the same hand, are long-standing questions.
Job.setting: The narrative is set in the land of Uz, outside Israel, and features a non-Israelite protagonist, giving it a deliberately universal cast. It addresses an audience wrestling with the justice of suffering rather than a specific historical occasion. Its patriarchal-seeming setting distances the story from any fixed period.
Job.themes: Job probes the problem of innocent suffering and the adequacy of conventional wisdom that ties fortune to conduct. Its literary character joins a folktale-like frame to extended, highly wrought poetic dialogue and climactic speeches from the whirlwind. Themes of divine justice, human limitation, and the limits of explanation dominate, and the book resists tidy resolution.
outline: The speeches from the whirlwind and epilogue (38–42)

Ps.name: Psalms
Ps.blurb: A collection of one hundred fifty poems and songs used in worship. Arranged in five books, it spans praise, lament, thanksgiving, and instruction, and is quoted throughout the New Testament.
Ps.attribution: The superscriptions attribute many psalms to David and others to figures such as Asaph, the Korahites, Solomon, and Moses, while some are anonymous. Critical scholarship treats these headings as traditional ascriptions rather than firm records of authorship and dates the individual psalms across a broad span, from the monarchy to the post-exilic period. The collection reached its final five-book shape late in that process.
Ps.setting: The psalms arise from and address the worship life of Israel, both communal and individual, across many centuries. Some reflect the temple and monarchy, others the experience of exile and its aftermath. The collection served as a hymnbook and prayer book for a worshipping community rather than addressing a single occasion.
Ps.themes: The Psalter gathers a wide range of poetic types, including hymns of praise, laments, thanksgivings, royal psalms, and wisdom poems. Its concerns span the whole of religious experience, from anguish and complaint to trust and exuberant praise, expressed through the parallelism and imagery of Hebrew verse. The five-book arrangement and framing psalms give the collection an overarching shape.

Prov.name: Proverbs
Prov.blurb: A book of wisdom literature gathering short sayings and longer poems on practical and moral conduct. Its material ranges from parental instruction to concise aphorisms on wisdom and folly, and it is a central text of the Old Testament wisdom tradition.
Prov.attribution: The book associates much of its material with Solomon and names further contributors, including collectors under Hezekiah and figures called Agur and Lemuel. Critical scholarship regards it as an anthology assembled over a long period, with the collections drawn together and edited in the post-exilic era, while individual sayings may be considerably older. Solomonic authorship is treated as a traditional attribution rather than a settled fact.
Prov.setting: Proverbs reflects the world of instruction, whether familial, scribal, or courtly, aimed at forming character and prudence. It addresses learners, often figured as a young person, being trained in wise living. The book's setting is educational and social rather than tied to specific events.
Prov.themes: Proverbs presents wisdom as skill in living rightly, contrasting it repeatedly with folly. Its concerns include speech, work, wealth, relationships, and self-control, expressed through pithy parallel sayings and extended poems, notably the personification of Wisdom. The collection assumes a broad correlation between wise conduct and well-being, tempered elsewhere in the wisdom corpus.
outline: The value of wisdom: extended instructions (1–9)
Further Solomonic proverbs collected under Hezekiah (25–29)
The words of Agur and Lemuel; the capable wife (30–31)

Eccl.name: Ecclesiastes
Eccl.blurb: A reflective work of wisdom literature presented in the voice of a teacher called Qoheleth. It examines the limits of human effort and understanding and the fleeting nature of earthly pursuits, and its meditations on meaning and mortality set it apart within the wisdom books.
Eccl.attribution: The book's speaker presents himself as a son of David and king in Jerusalem, a self-description that tradition read as Solomon. On linguistic grounds most critical scholars date the writing well after Solomon, commonly to the post-exilic or Hellenistic period, roughly the third century BCE, and treat the royal persona as a literary device. The two views frame the debate over its origin.
Eccl.setting: Ecclesiastes reflects on the human condition in broad terms rather than addressing a datable event, though its outlook is often linked to the intellectual currents of the Persian or Hellenistic era. It addresses readers grappling with the apparent transience and inequity of life. The royal voice provides a vantage of wide experience.
Eccl.themes: The book is a sustained meditation on the fleeting and elusive character of human striving, captured in its recurring term often rendered vanity or vapor. Its concerns include the limits of wisdom, the certainty of death, the value of ordinary enjoyment, and the inscrutability of events. Its questioning, at times skeptical tone makes it distinctive among the wisdom writings.
outline: The search for meaning in pleasure and toil (2–6)
Reflections and counsel on wise living (7–11)

Song.name: Song of Solomon
Song.blurb: A collection of love poetry celebrating mutual desire between two lovers in lyrical, imagistic language. It proceeds through exchanged speeches rather than a single narrative, and has drawn a long history of both literal and allegorical readings.
Song.attribution: The title links the work to Solomon, a connection tradition took as authorship. Critical scholarship generally treats this as an attribution and dates the poetry variously, with many placing its composition in the post-exilic period on linguistic grounds, while noting that it may gather older love lyrics. Whether it is a unified poem or an anthology is also debated.
Song.setting: The poems evoke pastoral and urban scenes of courtship rather than a defined historical occasion. They address, or give voice to, lovers in mutual longing, and have been read in worship communities in ways far removed from that surface sense. The setting is lyrical and idealized rather than tied to events.
Song.themes: The Song celebrates romantic and physical love through richly sensory imagery drawn from nature, agriculture, and the body. Its literary character is a sequence of dialogues and descriptive poems marked by mutuality between the voices. Historically it has attracted allegorical interpretation in both Jewish and Christian traditions, alongside more recent literal readings.

Isa.name: Isaiah
Isa.blurb: A major prophetic book spanning judgment against Judah and the nations and extended passages of consolation and restoration. Its composition and unity are matters of scholarly debate, and it is among the most frequently quoted Old Testament books in the New Testament.
Isa.attribution: Tradition attributes the whole book to Isaiah of Jerusalem in the eighth century BCE. Since the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries much critical scholarship has distinguished multiple layers, commonly a First Isaiah rooted in the eighth century, a Second Isaiah addressing the Babylonian exile in the sixth century, and a Third Isaiah reflecting the return, while other scholars defend a stronger unity. The debate over authorship and dating remains central to study of the book.
Isa.setting: The book's oracles address Judah and Jerusalem across a long historical arc, from the Assyrian threat, through the Babylonian exile, to the prospect of restoration. Its varied settings correspond to the layers scholars identify within it. The audience shifts from a kingdom under military pressure to a people in and beyond exile.
Isa.themes: Isaiah joins searing oracles of judgment to soaring visions of comfort and renewal. Its concerns include the holiness and sovereignty of the deity, trust rather than political alliance, judgment on pride, and the hope of restoration, including servant figures whose identity is much discussed. Its poetry is among the most influential in the prophetic corpus.

Jer.name: Jeremiah
Jer.blurb: A major prophetic book combining oracles, biography, and poetry set in Judah's final decades before the Babylonian exile. It records his warnings of judgment, his conflicts with authorities, and his promise of a new covenant, and is one of the longest books in the Bible.
Jer.attribution: The book presents its oracles as those of Jeremiah, active from the late seventh into the early sixth century BCE, and refers to their dictation to the scribe Baruch. Critical scholarship distinguishes poetic oracles, prose narratives about the prophet, and prose sermons in a Deuteronomistic style, seeing the book as growing through stages of editing after Jeremiah's lifetime. The Hebrew and Greek forms of the book also differ notably in length and order.
Jer.setting: The book is set in Judah during its last decades and the onset of the Babylonian exile, extending to the community left in the land and to those taken to Babylon. It addresses an audience living through national collapse and its aftermath. The looming and then realized destruction of Jerusalem dominates its horizon.
Jer.themes: Jeremiah interweaves prophetic poetry, personal lament, and narrative about the prophet's sufferings. Its concerns include persistent unfaithfulness and coming judgment, the anguish of the prophet, and, beyond catastrophe, the promise of restoration and a new covenant. The book's blend of biography and oracle gives it an unusually personal texture.
outline: Call and early oracles against Judah (1–25)
Narratives of conflict and the prophet's suffering (26–29)
The fall of Jerusalem and its aftermath (34–45)

Lam.name: Lamentations
Lam.blurb: A book of poetic laments over the destruction of Jerusalem. It consists of five poems, most of them acrostics following the Hebrew alphabet, giving sustained voice to grief and appeals for mercy amid catastrophe.
Lam.attribution: Tradition ascribes Lamentations to Jeremiah, and the Greek and later versions prefixed a note to that effect. Critical scholarship generally treats the book as anonymous, composed by one or more poets in the wake of Jerusalem's fall in 586 BCE, and questions the Jeremianic attribution on grounds of style and outlook. A sixth-century date near the events is widely accepted.
Lam.setting: The poems respond directly to the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and its temple and the suffering that followed. They address a community stunned by catastrophe and grappling with its meaning. The ruined city itself is the focus throughout.
Lam.themes: Lamentations gives structured expression to communal grief, moving between description of devastation, confession, and appeals for compassion. Its literary character is shaped by the acrostic form and the conventions of the lament. Themes of loss, mourning, acknowledgment of guilt, and a fragile hope of mercy run through the five poems.
outline: The day of the Lord's anger (2)
A voice of suffering and hope (3)

Ezek.name: Ezekiel
Ezek.blurb: A major prophetic book addressed to the exiles in Babylon and marked by elaborate visions and symbolic acts. It moves from oracles of judgment against Jerusalem to visions of restoration and a rebuilt temple, and its imagery has been widely influential in later texts.
Ezek.attribution: The book presents itself as the visions and oracles of Ezekiel, a priest among the Babylonian exiles in the early sixth century BCE, and is dated by a series of precise notices. Much critical scholarship accepts a substantial core going back to the prophet while recognizing later editing and expansion. The degree of that editing is debated, but the sixth-century exilic setting is broadly agreed.
Ezek.setting: The book is set among the Judean exiles in Babylonia, with its gaze fixed on the fate of Jerusalem and the exiled community. It addresses people displaced from their homeland and reckoning with the loss of temple and city. The dated visions anchor the oracles to this exilic situation.
Ezek.themes: Ezekiel is distinguished by dramatic visions, symbolic actions, and elaborate imagery. Its concerns include the departure and return of the divine presence, individual and communal responsibility, judgment on Jerusalem and the nations, and a detailed vision of a restored temple and land. The book's surreal imagery, including the opening chariot vision and the valley of dry bones, is among the most striking in the prophets.
outline: Call and visions of judgment on Jerusalem (1–24)
Restoration and the return of the presence (34–39)
The vision of the new temple (40–48)

Dan.name: Daniel
Dan.blurb: A book combining court narratives and apocalyptic visions, set among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. The first half recounts episodes of faithfulness under foreign kings, and the second reports symbolic visions of successive kingdoms; its apocalyptic imagery is echoed in the New Testament.
Dan.attribution: Tradition presents the book as the work of Daniel in the sixth century BCE. Many critical scholars, noting its detailed reflection of second-century events and its language, date the visions to the crisis under Antiochus IV around 165 BCE and view the court tales as older material collected and reframed. The traditional sixth-century dating and the critical second-century dating are the principal alternatives.
Dan.setting: The narratives are set at the courts of Babylonian and Persian kings, while the visions look toward a sequence of empires. On the critical reading the book addresses Judeans undergoing persecution in the Hellenistic period, encouraging endurance. The experience of living faithfully under foreign rule frames both halves.
Dan.themes: Daniel joins didactic court stories to apocalyptic visions of history and its end. Its concerns include fidelity under pressure, the sovereignty claimed over human kingdoms, and the succession and downfall of empires depicted through symbolic beasts and numbers. It is a principal source of later apocalyptic imagery. Portions of the book are written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.
outline: Vision of the ram and goat (8)
The final visions of conflict and end (10–12)

Hos.name: Hosea
Hos.blurb: The first of the twelve Minor Prophets, addressed to the northern kingdom of Israel before its fall. The book uses the imagery of marriage and infidelity to frame its message of judgment and restoration, and several of its lines are quoted in the New Testament.
Hos.attribution: The book is attributed to Hosea, active in the northern kingdom in the eighth century BCE before its fall to Assyria in 722 BCE. Critical scholarship accepts a core going back to the prophet while recognizing later Judean editing, including additions that apply the message to the south. The eighth-century setting of the original oracles is generally agreed.
Hos.setting: Hosea addresses the northern kingdom of Israel in its final decades, amid political instability and the growing Assyrian threat. Its audience is a prosperous but, in the prophet's view, unfaithful society on the brink of collapse. Later touches direct the message to Judah as well.
Hos.themes: Hosea frames the relationship between deity and people through the extended metaphor of marriage, infidelity, and reconciliation. Its concerns include covenant unfaithfulness figured as adultery, coming judgment, and an enduring, wounded love that reaches toward restoration. The book's emotive imagery and abrupt shifts of tone are characteristic.
outline: Love, judgment, and the call to return (11–14)

Joel.name: Joel
Joel.blurb: A short prophetic book occasioned by a devastating locust plague treated as a sign of a coming day of the LORD. It calls for communal repentance and promises renewal and an outpouring of the Spirit.
Joel.attribution: The book is attributed to Joel, of whom little is known. Because it contains few datable references, scholarly estimates of its origin range widely, from the pre-exilic monarchy to the post-exilic Persian period, with many favoring a post-exilic date. The uncertainty is unusually large and remains unresolved.
Joel.setting: The book responds to a severe locust plague and drought affecting Judah and its temple worship. Its audience is a community facing agricultural and cultic crisis, summoned to lamentation and repentance. The temple and its offerings figure prominently in the appeal.
Joel.themes: Joel moves from a present calamity to the wider theme of the day of the LORD, both as judgment and as deliverance. Its concerns include communal repentance, restoration of the land, and a promised outpouring of the divine spirit on all people. The book's vivid depiction of the locust invasion shades into cosmic imagery.
outline: The locust plague and call to lament (1)
The day of the Lord and call to return (2)
Judgment on the nations and Judah's restoration (3)

Amos.name: Amos
Amos.blurb: A prophetic book from Amos, a herdsman from Judah who prophesied against the northern kingdom of Israel in a time of prosperity. It delivers oracles against surrounding nations and Israel alike, with a strong emphasis on social justice, and is among the earliest of the writing prophets.
Amos.attribution: The book is attributed to Amos, a shepherd and cultivator from Tekoa in Judah who prophesied in the north in the mid-eighth century BCE. Scholars widely regard much of the material as going back to the prophet, with some later editing, including a closing note of restoration that some assign to a later hand. The eighth-century date of the core is broadly accepted.
Amos.setting: Amos addresses the northern kingdom of Israel during a period of prosperity and military security under Jeroboam II. Its audience includes the well-off and the religious establishment at sanctuaries such as Bethel. The prophet, an outsider from the south, confronts a confident society.
Amos.themes: Amos is marked by a forceful concern for social justice and the treatment of the poor. Its oracles indict economic exploitation, corrupt worship, and complacency, warning that ritual without justice invites judgment. Themes of the day of the LORD, divine sovereignty over the nations, and, at the close, restoration structure the book.
outline: Oracles against the nations and Israel (1–2)

Obad.name: Obadiah
Obad.blurb: The shortest book in the Old Testament, a single chapter of prophecy. It pronounces judgment against Edom for its hostility toward Judah, and closes with a brief announcement of restoration for the house of Jacob.
Obad.attribution: The book is attributed to Obadiah, otherwise unknown. Most scholars connect its central oracle to the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall in 586 BCE, when Edom was remembered as having taken advantage of Judah's collapse, placing composition in the sixth century BCE. Some material may be older, and precise dating is limited by the book's brevity.
Obad.setting: The oracle addresses the enmity between Judah and neighboring Edom, sharpened by Edom's conduct during Jerusalem's destruction. Its audience is a Judean community nursing the memory of betrayal by a kindred people. The book presupposes the catastrophe of the exile.
Obad.themes: Obadiah is a single sustained oracle of judgment against a hostile neighbor, closing with a turn toward restoration. Its concerns include retribution for pride and violence, the day of the LORD extended to the nations, and the eventual vindication of the house of Jacob. Its brevity gives it a concentrated, pointed character.
outline: The day of the Lord and Israel's restoration (15–21)

Jonah.name: Jonah
Jonah.blurb: A narrative among the Minor Prophets, centered on the prophet Jonah and his reluctant mission to the city of Nineveh. Unlike most prophetic books, it is chiefly a story about the prophet rather than a collection of oracles, and its account of the great fish is among the most widely known in Scripture.
Jonah.attribution: The book concerns a prophet named Jonah, mentioned elsewhere as active in the eighth century BCE, but it is written anonymously about him rather than by him. Many critical scholars date the composition to the post-exilic period, reading it as a didactic tale, while others argue for an earlier origin. Its genre and historicity are debated, with a range of views held in mainstream scholarship.
Jonah.setting: The story moves from Israel to the sea and to the Assyrian city of Nineveh, a symbol of a great foreign power. On the common reading it addresses a post-exilic audience reflecting on the reach of divine mercy beyond Israel. The Assyrian capital functions as the setting for the book's central question.
Jonah.themes: Jonah is a compact narrative marked by irony and reversal, focused on the prophet's resistance and its consequences. Its concerns include the possibility of repentance among outsiders, the scope of compassion, and the prophet's own recalcitrance. The book poses a pointed question about mercy rather than issuing conventional oracles.
outline: Jonah's anger and the lesson of the plant (4)

Mic.name: Micah
Mic.blurb: A prophetic book from Micah, a contemporary of Isaiah, addressing both Israel and Judah. It alternates oracles of judgment with passages of hope, touching on justice, leadership, and future restoration, and several of its verses are quoted or alluded to in the New Testament.
Mic.attribution: The book is attributed to Micah of Moresheth, active in Judah in the late eighth century BCE, a contemporary of Isaiah. Scholars generally accept a core of eighth-century oracles while assigning some passages, particularly certain words of hope, to later editing. The extent of later material is debated, but an eighth-century core is widely affirmed.
Mic.setting: Micah addresses Judah and the northern kingdom amid the Assyrian threat and internal social injustice. Its audience includes both the leadership and the ordinary people of a society the prophet charges with oppression. The impending fate of Samaria and the danger to Jerusalem frame the oracles.
Mic.themes: Micah alternates announcements of judgment with promises of restoration, giving the book a rhythm of doom and hope. Its concerns include social justice, the abuse of power by leaders and prophets, and expectations of future deliverance and peace. Its call to do justice and walk humbly is among the most cited lines in the prophets.
outline: Restoration and the ruler from Bethlehem (4–5)
The Lord's case against the people (6)

Nah.name: Nahum
Nah.blurb: A prophetic book consisting of poetry announcing the downfall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. It portrays the collapse of a power that had oppressed Israel and Judah, and its vivid imagery forms a sustained oracle against a single city.
Nah.attribution: The book is attributed to Nahum of Elkosh, otherwise unknown. Its subject, the fall of Nineveh in 612 BCE, places its composition in the late seventh century BCE, whether shortly before or after that event; scholars differ on the precise timing. The core is generally regarded as the work of a single prophet.
Nah.setting: Nahum addresses the anticipated destruction of Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian empire that had dominated the region. Its audience is a Judean community that had suffered under Assyrian power. The imminent collapse of that empire is the occasion of the oracle.
Nah.themes: Nahum is a tightly focused poetic oracle celebrating the downfall of an oppressive power. Its concerns include divine judgment on cruelty and pride, the reversal of an empire's fortunes, and vindication for those it had crushed. The book's imagery of siege and ruin is vivid and unrelenting.
outline: A hymn on the Lord's power (1)
The siege and fall of Nineveh (2)

Hab.name: Habakkuk
Hab.blurb: A short prophetic book structured as a dialogue between the prophet and God over the problem of injustice and impending invasion. It concludes with a psalm-like prayer, and one of its lines on living by faith is quoted several times in the New Testament.
Hab.attribution: The book is attributed to Habakkuk, of whom nothing is known beyond the title. Its references to the rising Babylonian threat point to a composition around the late seventh century BCE, before or near the Babylonian ascendancy. A core from this period is generally accepted, with the closing psalm sometimes discussed as a separate piece.
Hab.setting: Habakkuk is set on the eve of the Babylonian advance, as the prophet confronts violence within Judah and the menace of a foreign conqueror. Its audience faces the prospect of invasion and the moral difficulty of divine use of a ruthless power. The looming Babylonian threat frames the dialogue.
Hab.themes: The book takes the form of a complaint and response, wrestling with why injustice persists and why judgment comes through a violent nation. Its concerns include theodicy, faithful endurance amid crisis, and eventual judgment on the oppressor. It moves from protest to a closing prayer of trust.
outline: The prophet's complaints and the Lord's answers (1–2)
The just shall live by faith (2)

Zeph.name: Zephaniah
Zeph.blurb: A prophetic book set in the reign of Josiah of Judah, announcing a coming day of judgment against Judah and the nations. It moves from warnings of desolation to a closing promise of restoration for a humbled remnant, and belongs to the collection of twelve Minor Prophets.
Zeph.attribution: The book is attributed to Zephaniah and set in the reign of Josiah, placing it in the late seventh century BCE. Scholars generally accept a seventh-century core, with some passages, particularly the closing words of hope, sometimes assigned to later editing. The Josianic setting given in the title is widely followed.
Zeph.setting: Zephaniah addresses Judah under Josiah, before or during that king's religious reforms, amid concern over foreign cults and social conduct. Its audience is a community warned of imminent judgment. The book's horizon extends from Judah to the surrounding nations.
Zeph.themes: Zephaniah is dominated by the theme of the day of the LORD as a sweeping judgment. Its concerns include condemnation of idolatry and complacency, judgment on the nations, and a final turn toward the preservation and restoration of a humble remnant. The movement from near-universal judgment to hope structures the whole.
outline: The coming day of judgment on Judah (1)
Promise of restoration for the remnant (3)

Hag.name: Haggai
Hag.blurb: A brief post-exilic prophetic book addressed to the community that had returned from Babylon. Its dated oracles urge the people to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, and it is closely tied in setting to the book of Zechariah.
Hag.attribution: The book is attributed to Haggai and precisely dated to the second year of the Persian king Darius, around 520 BCE. Scholars broadly accept this setting, seeing the oracles as reflecting the early restoration period, with the third-person framing suggesting compilation by an editor. The dating is among the most secure in the prophetic corpus.
Hag.setting: Haggai addresses the community that had returned from Babylonian exile, gathered around the leaders Zerubbabel and Joshua, at a time when the temple lay unbuilt. Its audience is a struggling community facing economic hardship and discouragement. The rebuilding of the temple is the immediate occasion.
Hag.themes: Haggai is a series of short, dated oracles urging the completion of the temple. Its concerns include the priority of rebuilding the sanctuary, the connection drawn between neglect and hardship, and encouragement toward future glory for the house and its leaders. The book's brevity and precise dating give it an almost documentary character.
outline: The promised glory of the new house (2)
A word on purity and blessing (2)

Zech.name: Zechariah
Zech.blurb: A post-exilic prophetic book combining a series of symbolic night visions with later oracles. It encourages the rebuilding of the temple and looks toward future restoration, and its imagery is frequently drawn upon in the New Testament, especially in the passion accounts.
Zech.attribution: The opening chapters are dated to the reign of Darius around 520 BCE and attributed to Zechariah, a contemporary of Haggai. Critical scholarship widely distinguishes these chapters from the later chapters, often called Second Zechariah, which many assign to a different and later hand on grounds of style and content. The composite character of the book is a standard feature of its study.
Zech.setting: The first part addresses the early post-exilic community engaged in rebuilding the temple under Persian rule. The later chapters, harder to date, look toward broader future expectations. The audience is a restoration community reflecting on its present struggles and its hopes.
Zech.themes: Zechariah joins symbolic night visions and oracles encouraging the restoration to later, more apocalyptic material about future conflict and deliverance. Its concerns include the rebuilding of the temple, the roles of civil and priestly leaders, and eschatological hope. Its imagery of a coming king and a stricken shepherd is frequently reused in the New Testament passion narratives.
outline: Oracle against the nations and the coming king (9–11)
The final oracle: conflict and deliverance (12–14)

Mal.name: Malachi
Mal.blurb: The last of the Minor Prophets and the final book of the Old Testament in the Christian canon. It is structured as a series of disputations addressing priestly neglect, covenant faithfulness, and social conduct, and closes with an expectation of a coming messenger.
Mal.attribution: The name Malachi means my messenger, and scholars debate whether it is a personal name or a title drawn from the book's own words. Its concerns point to the Persian post-exilic period, commonly the fifth century BCE, after the temple had been rebuilt. A single author for the core is generally assumed, whatever the meaning of the name.
Mal.setting: Malachi addresses a post-exilic community in Judah at a time of religious laxity, cultic neglect, and social strain. Its audience is a settled community whose enthusiasm for worship and covenant has, in the prophet's view, cooled. The functioning but poorly served temple forms the backdrop.
Mal.themes: Malachi is cast as a series of disputations in which charges are raised, objections voiced, and answers given. Its concerns include the integrity of worship and priesthood, faithfulness in marriage and dealings, tithing, and the coming day of reckoning. The closing expectation of a messenger who prepares the way rounds off the collection and, in the Christian ordering, the Old Testament.
outline: The Lord's love and the priests' failures (1–2)
The coming messenger and day of judgment (3)
A final call and the promise of Elijah (4)

Matt.name: Matthew
Matt.blurb: The first of the four Gospels, presenting an account of the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. It gives particular attention to his teaching, gathered into extended discourses, and frequently cites the Old Testament, standing at the opening of the New Testament.
Matt.attribution: Early tradition attributes the Gospel to Matthew, one of the twelve. Most critical scholars regard it as anonymous and composed later in the first century, commonly around 80 to 90 CE, by an author drawing on Mark and other sources. The traditional and critical positions differ over both authorship and date, though a first-century origin is not in dispute.
Matt.setting: The Gospel is widely thought to address a community with strong Jewish-Christian roots, plausibly in Syria, concerned with the relationship between Jesus and the Jewish scriptures and tradition. Its frequent appeal to fulfillment of prophecy suits such a setting. The audience is engaged with questions of continuity between the new movement and Israel's heritage.
Matt.themes: Matthew organizes much of Jesus' teaching into five major discourses and stresses the fulfillment of the scriptures. Its concerns include Jesus as teacher and awaited figure, the shape of the community that follows him, and continuity with Israel's law and prophets. The Gospel's structured teaching sections and formula quotations are distinctive features.
outline: Beginnings and the Sermon on the Mount (3–7)

Mark.name: Mark
Mark.blurb: The shortest of the four Gospels, narrating the ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus in a rapid, action-focused style. It is widely regarded in scholarship as among the earliest of the Gospels, and shares much of its material with Matthew and Luke.
Mark.attribution: Tradition attributes the Gospel to Mark, associated with Peter. Critical scholarship treats it as formally anonymous and, on the common two-source theory, as the earliest of the Synoptic Gospels, generally dated around 65 to 75 CE. Its priority is a widely held but not universal scholarly position.
Mark.setting: The Gospel is often thought to address a community facing hardship or persecution, with Rome frequently proposed as its place of origin. Its emphasis on suffering and discipleship suits an audience under pressure. The precise location is inferred rather than stated.
Mark.themes: Mark is fast-paced and vivid, moving briskly through Jesus' deeds with a recurring sense of urgency. Its concerns include the identity of Jesus disclosed gradually, the centrality of the cross, and the difficulty of true discipleship. Motifs of secrecy about Jesus' identity and the failures of his followers are characteristic, and the abrupt ending has drawn much discussion.
outline: The way to Jerusalem and passion predictions (8–10)

Luke.name: Luke
Luke.blurb: A Gospel addressed to a reader named Theophilus and written as an orderly account of the life of Jesus. It gives notable attention to the marginalized, to prayer, and to birth narratives found nowhere else, forming the first part of a two-volume work continued in Acts.
Luke.attribution: Tradition attributes the Gospel to Luke, a companion of Paul. Most critical scholars regard it as anonymous, written later in the first century, commonly around 80 to 90 CE, by an author who used Mark and other sources. Luke and Acts are widely held to be two volumes by the same writer.
Luke.setting: The Gospel is addressed to Theophilus and is generally taken to have a broadly Gentile-oriented readership in the wider Greco-Roman world. Its concern with outsiders and the poor suits a mixed audience beyond Judea. The two-volume design links the story of Jesus to the spread of the movement that follows.
Luke.themes: Luke presents an orderly narrative with careful attention to setting the story within its wider history. Its concerns include compassion toward the poor, outsiders, and women, the importance of prayer and the Spirit, and reversal of social expectations. Distinctive parables and infancy narratives give the Gospel much of its character.

John.name: John
John.blurb: The fourth Gospel, distinct in style and content from the other three. It organizes its account around a series of signs and extended discourses, with sustained reflection on the identity of Jesus; its authorship and setting are debated among scholars.
John.attribution: Tradition links the Gospel to John, often identified with the beloved disciple. Critical scholarship generally regards it as anonymous, the product of a distinct community and perhaps successive stages of composition, commonly dated around 90 to 100 CE. Both authorship and the process of composition are actively debated.
John.setting: The Gospel is often associated with a particular Christian community whose distinctive outlook it reflects, though its precise location is uncertain. Its extended reflection on Jesus' identity suggests an audience engaged in defining that identity, at times in tension with a surrounding synagogue setting. The community context is inferred from the text's emphases.
John.themes: John differs markedly from the other Gospels in structure, vocabulary, and tone. Its concerns include the identity and origin of Jesus, expressed through signs, discourses, and symbolic language, and themes of light, life, truth, and belief. The seven signs and the extended farewell discourses are among its defining features.

Acts.name: Acts
Acts.blurb: A historical narrative serving as a sequel to Luke's Gospel and tracing the spread of the early church after the ascension of Jesus. It follows the growth of the movement from Jerusalem outward, centering on Peter and then Paul, providing the principal narrative bridge between the Gospels and the letters.
Acts.attribution: Acts is traditionally attributed, with the third Gospel, to Luke. Most scholars accept the common authorship of Luke and Acts and date the work to the late first century, commonly around 80 to 90 CE. Whether the author was a companion of Paul, as tradition holds, is debated in light of differences from Paul's own letters.
Acts.setting: The narrative moves from Jerusalem through the wider Mediterranean world to Rome, following the early movement as it crosses cultural and geographic boundaries. It addresses a readership interested in how the movement grew from a Jewish setting into a broader mission. The Roman imperial world provides the stage.
Acts.themes: Acts is a narrative of expansion, tracing the movement's spread from Jerusalem to the empire's capital. Its concerns include the role of the Spirit in guiding the mission, the inclusion of Gentiles, and the relationship of the movement to Jewish and Roman authorities. Speeches and travel narratives structure the account, with Peter dominating the first half and Paul the second.
outline: Paul's first missionary journey and the council (13–15)
Paul's arrest and journey to Rome (21–28)

Rom.name: Romans
Rom.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Rome and the most systematic of Paul's epistles. It sets out an extended argument concerning sin, faith, law, and the inclusion of Jews and Gentiles, quotes the Old Testament extensively, and has been widely influential in later theology.
Rom.attribution: Romans is one of the letters almost universally accepted as written by Paul, generally dated to the mid- to late 50s CE. It names Tertius as the scribe who wrote it down. Its Pauline authorship is among the most secure in the New Testament.
Rom.setting: Paul writes to a community in Rome he had not yet visited, apparently as he plans a journey westward and seeks the support of that church. The letter addresses a congregation of both Jewish and Gentile believers navigating their relationship to one another. Its occasion is partly introductory and partly to set out his message in advance of a visit.
Rom.themes: Romans develops a sustained argument on the human predicament and its resolution, the relationship of law and faith, and the standing of Jews and Gentiles together. Its concerns include righteousness, the place of Israel, and the ethical shape of communal life. The letter's systematic scope and heavy use of scripture have made it especially influential in the history of interpretation.
outline: The human predicament and righteousness by faith (1–4)
Life in the Spirit and the place of Israel (5–11)

1Cor.name: 1 Corinthians
1Cor.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Corinth in response to reports and questions from that community. It treats divisions, conduct, worship, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection, and is among the most detailed windows into an early Christian congregation.
1Cor.attribution: First Corinthians is widely accepted as a genuine letter of Paul, generally dated to the mid-50s CE during his time in Ephesus. It refers to earlier correspondence and to reports Paul had received. Its Pauline authorship is not seriously contested.
1Cor.setting: Paul writes to the church he had founded in the cosmopolitan port city of Corinth, responding to news of divisions and to a list of questions the community had raised. The audience is a diverse congregation grappling with tensions over status, conduct, and practice. The urban, socially mixed setting shapes many of the issues addressed.
1Cor.themes: First Corinthians addresses a series of concrete problems in community life. Its concerns include unity amid factions, sexual and social ethics, order in worship, the exercise of spiritual gifts, and the resurrection of the dead. The letter's practical, case-by-case character, including its extended treatment of love and of resurrection, is distinctive.

2Cor.name: 2 Corinthians
2Cor.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Corinth and notably personal in tone. It defends Paul's ministry, discusses a collection for the church in Jerusalem, and reflects on hardship and reconciliation.
2Cor.attribution: Second Corinthians is accepted as Pauline, generally dated to the mid-50s CE. Its abrupt shifts of tone have led many scholars to propose that it combines more than one letter or letter fragment, though others read it as a unity. This question of composition is a notable feature of its study.
2Cor.setting: Paul writes again to the Corinthian church amid strained relations, following painful exchanges and the arrival of rival teachers. The audience is a community whose loyalty to Paul had been tested. The letter's occasion includes both reconciliation and the defense of his standing.
2Cor.themes: Second Corinthians is the most personal and emotionally charged of Paul's letters. Its concerns include the nature of authentic ministry, suffering and consolation, generosity in the collection for Jerusalem, and the defense of his authority against opponents. The letter's shifts between warmth, appeal, and sharp self-defense give it a distinctive intensity.

Gal.name: Galatians
Gal.blurb: A letter addressed to churches in Galatia and marked by a sharp, argumentative tone. It concerns the relationship between faith, law, and the status of Gentile believers, and shares much of its subject matter with the letter to the Romans.
Gal.attribution: Galatians is universally accepted as a letter of Paul, though scholars debate its exact date and the identity of its recipients, which bears on whether it is among his earliest or middle letters. Estimates commonly range across the late 40s to the mid-50s CE. Its authenticity is not in question.
Gal.setting: Paul writes to churches in Galatia after other teachers had urged Gentile believers to adopt observance of the Jewish law. The audience is a group of congregations whose understanding of their status Paul regards as endangered. The controversy over law observance is the letter's driving occasion.
Gal.themes: Galatians argues vigorously that Gentile believers are not required to take on the works of the law. Its concerns include the relationship of faith and law, freedom, and the marks of authentic community life in the Spirit. The letter's polemical urgency and autobiographical passages set it apart.
outline: Paul's defense of his gospel and calling (1–2)
Freedom and life in the Spirit (5–6)

Eph.name: Ephesians
Eph.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Ephesus, though its authorship is debated in scholarship. It moves from reflection on unity and the church to practical instruction on conduct and relationships, and is one of the epistles associated with Paul's imprisonment.
Eph.attribution: The letter presents itself as written by Paul from imprisonment. Many critical scholars question direct Pauline authorship on grounds of style, vocabulary, and thought, proposing composition by a later associate in the Pauline tradition, while others defend it as genuinely Paul's. The words identifying Ephesus are also absent from some early manuscripts, suggesting a possible circular letter.
Eph.setting: Whether addressed specifically to Ephesus or circulated more broadly, the letter speaks to Gentile believers about their place within a wider community. The audience is invited to reflect on unity across former divisions. The setting is presented as one of imprisonment for the sake of the message.
Eph.themes: Ephesians reflects on the unity of a diverse community and the reconciliation of divided groups. Its concerns include cosmic scope, the character of the church, and practical instruction on conduct, relationships, and household order. The letter's elevated, liturgical style and its closing imagery of spiritual armor are characteristic.
outline: Blessing and the purpose of unity (1–2)
Exhortation to unity and new conduct (4–5)

Phil.name: Philippians
Phil.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Philippi and warm in tone, written from imprisonment. It expresses thanks, encourages steadfastness and joy, and includes a well-known hymn-like passage; it is counted among the Pauline prison epistles.
Phil.attribution: Philippians is accepted as a genuine letter of Paul, written from imprisonment, though scholars debate whether the place of confinement was Rome, Ephesus, or elsewhere, which affects its dating. Some also propose that the letter combines more than one note. Its Pauline authorship, however, is secure.
Phil.setting: Paul writes to the church at Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia, with which he had a close and supportive relationship. The occasion includes thanks for their material help and encouragement amid difficulty. His own imprisonment forms the backdrop to the letter's reflections.
Phil.themes: Philippians is marked by warmth, gratitude, and a recurring note of joy despite hardship. Its concerns include partnership in a shared cause, steadfastness under pressure, humility modeled on Christ, and contentment. The letter's celebrated hymn-like passage on Christ's humility is among its best-known features.
outline: Warnings and the pursuit of the goal (3)

Col.name: Colossians
Col.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Colossae, with its authorship debated among scholars. It counters certain teachings circulating in the community and offers instruction on Christian conduct and household relationships, sharing much material with the letter to the Ephesians.
Col.attribution: The letter claims Paul as its author, writing from imprisonment. Scholarly opinion is divided: some accept it as genuinely Pauline, while others regard it as the work of a later follower on grounds of style and thought. Its close relationship to Ephesians figures in this debate.
Col.setting: The letter addresses the church at Colossae in Asia Minor, responding to teachings the author considers a threat to the community. The audience is a congregation being urged toward practices and beliefs the letter opposes. The nature of that teaching is described only through the letter's rebuttal.
Col.themes: Colossians counters a rival teaching by emphasizing the sufficiency and supremacy of Christ. Its concerns include the cosmic significance attributed to Christ, warnings against certain ascetic and ritual practices, and practical instruction on conduct and household relationships. The letter shares much of its ethical material with Ephesians.
outline: Thanksgiving and the supremacy of Christ (1)
The new life and its practices (3)

1Thess.name: 1 Thessalonians
1Thess.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Thessalonica and often regarded as among the earliest of Paul's epistles. It commends the community's faith, offers encouragement, and addresses questions about those who have died and the return of Christ; it is brief and largely pastoral in character.
1Thess.attribution: First Thessalonians is accepted as genuinely Pauline and is widely considered one of his earliest surviving letters, commonly dated around 50 to 51 CE. This would make it among the earliest writings in the New Testament. Its authenticity is not disputed.
1Thess.setting: Paul writes to a young church he had recently founded in the Macedonian city of Thessalonica, from which he had departed under pressure. The audience is a new community facing hardship and grief and holding questions about the future. The letter follows a report Paul had received about their situation.
1Thess.themes: First Thessalonians is warm and encouraging, reinforcing a recently established community. Its concerns include steadfastness under affliction, holy conduct, and reassurance regarding those who have died before the expected return of Christ. Its treatment of future hope and its pastoral tone are its most notable features.
outline: The return of Christ and final exhortations (4–5)

2Thess.name: 2 Thessalonians
2Thess.blurb: A letter addressed to the church at Thessalonica, with its authorship debated in scholarship. It responds to confusion about end-time expectations and urges steady conduct and work, closely paralleling the concerns of the first letter to that community.
2Thess.attribution: The letter presents itself as Paul's second letter to Thessalonica. Scholars are divided: some accept it as genuine, written soon after the first letter, while others see it as composed later in Paul's name, partly because of differences in its treatment of end-time expectation. The question remains open.
2Thess.setting: The letter addresses the Thessalonian community amid confusion and unsettlement over claims that a decisive day had already come or was imminent. The audience includes some who had reportedly stopped working in that expectation. The letter responds to this disturbance within the community.
2Thess.themes: Second Thessalonians seeks to correct misunderstanding about the timing of end-time events and to steady the community. Its concerns include endurance under persecution, a sequence of events expected before the end, and the importance of orderly conduct and continued work. Its eschatological instruction and its call to steady labor are its defining emphases.
outline: Events preceding the day of the Lord (2)

1Tim.name: 1 Timothy
1Tim.blurb: One of the Pastoral Epistles, addressed to Paul's associate Timothy. It offers guidance on church leadership, sound teaching, and conduct within the community, and is grouped with 2 Timothy and Titus as letters directed to individuals overseeing churches.
1Tim.attribution: First Timothy presents itself as written by Paul to Timothy. Many critical scholars regard the three Pastoral Epistles as composed after Paul's lifetime by a later writer in his name, citing distinctive vocabulary, developed church structures, and the difficulty of fitting them into Paul's known career, while others defend Pauline authorship. This is one of the more prominent authorship debates in the New Testament.
1Tim.setting: The letter is framed as guidance to Timothy, presented as overseeing the community at Ephesus. Its audience is concerned with the ordering of church life and with countering teaching the letter regards as false. The setting reflects communities developing structures of leadership and instruction.
1Tim.themes: First Timothy focuses on the ordering and oversight of communal life. Its concerns include sound teaching against error, qualifications for leaders, the conduct of worship, and the management of various groups within the community. Its attention to church offices and practical administration marks it and the other Pastorals.
outline: Duties toward groups in the church (5–6)

2Tim.name: 2 Timothy
2Tim.blurb: One of the Pastoral Epistles, addressed to Timothy. Framed as a final charge written from imprisonment, it urges endurance and faithful teaching, and is the most personal in tone of the three Pastoral letters.
2Tim.attribution: Like the other Pastorals, 2 Timothy presents itself as Paul's and is subject to the same debate over authorship, with many scholars assigning it to a later writer and others defending its authenticity. It is often noted as the most personal of the three and, on the traditional reading, the last. The dispute follows the same lines as for 1 Timothy and Titus.
2Tim.setting: The letter is cast as Paul's final charge to Timothy from imprisonment, anticipating the end of his life. Its audience, whether Timothy directly or communities reading over his shoulder, is urged to hold fast under pressure. The tone of impending departure shapes the whole.
2Tim.themes: Second Timothy reads as a testament, combining personal appeal with exhortation to perseverance. Its concerns include endurance amid suffering, faithful transmission of teaching, and warnings about difficult times and false teachers. Its intimate, valedictory tone distinguishes it from the more administrative first letter.

Titus.name: Titus
Titus.blurb: One of the Pastoral Epistles, addressed to Paul's associate Titus on the island of Crete. It gives instruction on appointing leaders and ordering the life of the churches there, sharing its concerns and vocabulary with the letters to Timothy.
Titus.attribution: Titus presents itself as written by Paul to his associate Titus. It is grouped with 1 and 2 Timothy as the Pastoral Epistles and shares in the same authorship debate, with scholars divided between Pauline authorship and later composition in his name. The arguments parallel those for the Timothy letters.
Titus.setting: The letter is framed as instruction to Titus, left to organize communities on the island of Crete. Its audience is concerned with appointing suitable leaders and addressing disorder and false teaching. The Cretan setting is invoked pointedly in the letter's characterizations.
Titus.themes: Titus concentrates on ordering community life and appointing sound leadership. Its concerns include qualifications for elders, the refutation of false teachers, and instruction on conduct for various groups. Its overlap in vocabulary and outlook with the Timothy letters is close.
outline: Conduct in society and final words (3)

Phlm.name: Philemon
