Phlm.blurb: A brief personal letter addressed to Philemon concerning Onesimus, an enslaved man connected to his household. It is the shortest of the Pauline epistles and is written as a personal appeal rather than a general teaching; it is counted among the letters associated with Paul's imprisonment.
Phlm.attribution: Philemon is universally accepted as a genuine letter of Paul, written from imprisonment. Its brevity and personal character make it one of the least disputed of his letters. It is commonly dated to the same period as his other prison letters.
Phlm.setting: Paul writes to Philemon, a householder whose enslaved man Onesimus had come into contact with Paul during his imprisonment. The letter appeals to Philemon regarding Onesimus's reception. Its occasion is a specific personal situation rather than a general controversy.
Phlm.themes: Philemon is a carefully worded personal appeal, notable for its tact and rhetorical delicacy. Its concerns include reconciliation, obligation, and the relationship between the parties, framed in terms of partnership and appeal rather than command. The letter offers a rare glimpse of Paul addressing a single private matter.

Heb.name: Hebrews
Heb.blurb: A letter or written sermon whose authorship is unknown and much debated, though it was long associated with Paul. It argues at length from the Old Testament, drawing extensively on the language of priesthood, sacrifice, and covenant, and quotes and interprets the Hebrew scriptures more densely than most New Testament books.
Heb.attribution: The authorship of Hebrews is unknown; the work is anonymous and lacks the usual letter opening. Ancient and modern proposals have ranged widely, and the traditional association with Paul was questioned even in antiquity and is now generally rejected by scholars. It is commonly dated to the later first century, though the exact time is uncertain.
Heb.setting: The work addresses a community, apparently of Jewish-Christian background, tempted to fall away under pressure. Its sustained argument from the scriptures and the sacrificial system suits readers steeped in that tradition. Whether written before or after the destruction of the temple in 70 CE is debated and bears on its setting.
Heb.themes: Hebrews reads more as a sustained sermon than a conventional letter, developing an extended argument from the Old Testament. Its concerns include the priesthood and sacrifice, the relationship between old and new covenants, and endurance in faith illustrated by past examples. Its dense scriptural exposition and its portrait of a great high priest are distinctive.

Jas.name: James
Jas.blurb: A general epistle offering practical instruction in the manner of wisdom literature. It addresses faith and conduct, speech, wealth and poverty, and endurance under trial, reading as a series of exhortations rather than a sustained argument.
Jas.attribution: The letter names James as its author, traditionally identified with James the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem community. Scholars are divided over whether it stems from him, perhaps early, or from a later writer using his name, with its polished Greek and general tone figuring in the debate. Both authorship and date remain contested.
Jas.setting: The letter is addressed broadly to dispersed communities rather than to a single congregation, giving it the character of a general or circular writing. Its audience faces trials, social inequality, and tensions between profession and practice. The setting is diffuse, in keeping with its wisdom-style content.
Jas.themes: James resembles wisdom literature, stringing together practical exhortations on right living. Its concerns include the integrity of faith expressed in action, the dangers of the tongue, the treatment of rich and poor, and patience under trial. Its aphoristic, loosely connected style distinguishes it from the argumentative letters.
outline: Warnings to the rich and calls to patience (4–5)

1Pet.name: 1 Peter
1Pet.blurb: A general epistle addressed to Christians in Asia Minor facing hardship. It encourages endurance under suffering and offers instruction on conduct within society and the household, drawing frequently on the language and imagery of the Old Testament.
1Pet.attribution: The letter presents itself as written by the apostle Peter. Some scholars accept this, perhaps with the help of a secretary, while others regard it as composed later in Peter's name, citing its refined Greek and apparent situation. The date and authorship are debated, though a first-century origin is generally assumed.
1Pet.setting: The letter addresses scattered communities in regions of Asia Minor undergoing social hostility and hardship. Its audience consists of believers described as resident aliens and strangers, facing pressure from their surrounding society. The experience of marginalization shapes the letter's counsel.
1Pet.themes: First Peter encourages endurance and holy conduct in the face of suffering. Its concerns include steadfastness under hostility, conduct within society and the household, and the shaping of identity as a distinct people. Its rich use of Old Testament imagery and its focus on suffering give it a consistent tone.
outline: A living hope and holy living (1–2)
Conduct in society and the household (2–3)

2Pet.name: 2 Peter
2Pet.blurb: A general epistle whose authorship is among the most debated in the New Testament. It warns against false teachers and addresses questions about the delay of Christ's return, sharing a substantial body of material with the letter of Jude.
2Pet.attribution: Second Peter claims the apostle Peter as its author, but its authenticity is questioned more widely than that of almost any other New Testament book. Many scholars regard it as among the latest writings in the collection, composed in Peter's name well after his lifetime, citing its style, its use of Jude, and its concerns. A minority defend traditional authorship.
2Pet.setting: The letter addresses communities troubled by teachers the author considers false and by doubt over the expected return of Christ. Its audience is unsettled by the passage of time and by challenges to inherited teaching. The setting reflects a later stage of communal life reckoning with delay and dissent.
2Pet.themes: Second Peter combines warning against error with reassurance about the future. Its concerns include the reliability of received teaching, condemnation of false teachers, and the certainty of a coming reckoning despite its apparent delay. Its overlap with Jude and its defense of tradition are notable features.
outline: Growth in faith and the reliability of the message (1)
The delay of the day of the Lord (3)

1John.name: 1 John
1John.blurb: A general epistle written to reassure its readers and to counter teachings the author regards as false. It emphasizes themes of love, truth, and the tests of genuine faith, reading more as a reflective address than a conventional letter, lacking the usual opening and closing forms.
1John.attribution: The work is anonymous but has traditionally been associated with John and is closely related in language and thought to the fourth Gospel. Scholars generally connect it with the same community or circle that produced that Gospel, dating it to the late first century, while debating whether the same person wrote both. Its precise authorship remains uncertain.
1John.setting: The writing addresses a community apparently divided by a schism, with some having departed over questions of belief and conduct. Its audience is urged to hold to what it had received against rival claims. The setting is one of internal conflict within a community sharing the outlook of the fourth Gospel.
1John.themes: First John reflects on the marks of authentic faith and belonging. Its concerns include love within the community, the reality of Christ's coming, and tests by which genuine faith may be recognized. Its circling, meditative style and its contrasts of light and darkness, truth and falsehood, are characteristic.
outline: Children of God and love for one another (2–3)
Testing the spirits and abiding in love (4)

2John.name: 2 John
2John.blurb: A very short letter addressed to a community described as the elect lady and her children. It urges mutual love and warns against deceptive teachers, and is one of the briefest books in the New Testament, occupying a single chapter.
2John.attribution: The letter is written by an author who identifies himself only as the elder and is traditionally associated with John and the Johannine circle. Scholars generally group it with 1 and 3 John as products of the same community, dating it to the late first century, though the identity of the elder is uncertain. Its brevity limits what can be said with confidence.
2John.setting: The letter addresses a community, figuratively called the elect lady and her children, amid concern over traveling teachers spreading views the author rejects. Its audience is warned about whom to welcome. The setting reflects the same conflicts over teaching seen in 1 John.
2John.themes: Second John distills the concerns of the Johannine letters into a brief note. Its themes include mutual love, adherence to received teaching, and caution toward deceivers. Despite its length it touches the community's central issues of truth and hospitality.

3John.name: 3 John
3John.blurb: A short personal letter addressed to an individual named Gaius. It commends hospitality toward traveling teachers and names a disputed figure in the community, and together with 2 John it is among the shortest books in the Bible.
3John.attribution: Like 2 John, this letter is written by one who calls himself the elder and is traditionally linked with John and the Johannine circle. Scholars associate the three Johannine letters with the same community and setting, dating them to the late first century, while leaving the elder's identity open. Its short length limits firm conclusions.
3John.setting: The letter is addressed to an individual named Gaius and concerns the reception of traveling teachers within the community. It refers to a figure named Diotrephes who had refused such hospitality. The setting is a concrete dispute over authority and welcome in a local community.
3John.themes: Third John concerns hospitality and conflict over leadership. Its themes include support for traveling workers, commendation and rebuke of named individuals, and the tension between rival figures in a community. It offers a rare, specific glimpse of an internal quarrel in an early congregation.

Jude.name: Jude
Jude.blurb: A brief general epistle occupying a single chapter. It warns against false teachers and urges its readers to contend for the faith, sharing much of its content with the second letter of Peter and referring to material outside the Old Testament canon.
Jude.attribution: The letter names Jude, described as a brother of James, traditionally understood as a brother of Jesus. Scholars are divided over whether it stems from that figure or was written later in his name, and its date is uncertain. Its literary relationship to 2 Peter, which shares much of its content, figures in the discussion.
Jude.setting: The letter addresses communities troubled by teachers whose conduct and teaching the author condemns. Its audience is urged to hold to received belief against these figures. The setting is one of perceived internal threat, described in vivid and allusive terms.
Jude.themes: Jude is a short, forceful warning against error. Its themes include contending for inherited teaching, condemnation of false teachers through a series of examples, and encouragement to persevere. Its use of imagery and its citation of writings outside the Old Testament canon are distinctive features.
outline: Greeting and the call to contend for the faith (1–4)
Examples and denunciation of the ungodly (5–16)
Exhortation to the faithful and closing doxology (17–25)

Rev.name: Revelation
Rev.blurb: The final book of the New Testament, an apocalypse written to seven churches in Asia Minor. It presents a sequence of visions in highly symbolic imagery concerning judgment, conflict, and a renewed creation, drawing heavily on the language and imagery of the Old Testament, especially the prophetic books.
Rev.attribution: The book names its author as John, and tradition often identified him with the apostle, though the writer describes himself simply as a servant and prophet. Scholars debate whether this John is the apostle, another figure of the same name, or a distinct prophet, and generally date the work to the late first century, commonly the reign of Domitian around 95 CE. An earlier date is also argued by some.
Rev.setting: The book addresses seven specific churches in the Roman province of Asia, amid pressures the author frames as conflict with imperial power and surrounding society. Its audience faces hostility and the temptation to accommodate. The Roman imperial context pervades its imagery.
Rev.themes: Revelation belongs to the apocalyptic genre, unfolding through visions rich in symbol and number. Its concerns include judgment, the conflict between opposing powers, faithful endurance, and the promise of a renewed creation. Its dense reuse of Old Testament imagery, especially from the prophets, and its long history of contested interpretation are defining features.
outline: Vision of the Son of Man and letters to the seven churches (1–3)
The throne, the scroll, and the seven seals (4–7)
Conflict, the beasts, and the bowls of wrath (12–18)
Final judgment and the new creation (19–22)
